plain_title: Pulling out your own hair and not being able to stop
one_liner: Repeatedly pulling out hair, causing hair loss, despite trying to stop.
in_simple_words: Trichotillomania is a body-focused repetitive behaviour: pulling hair from the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes, or elsewhere, often without fully noticing, sometimes in a focused way to relieve tension. It leads to bald patches or missing lashes that people go to great lengths to hide. It's not a habit someone can simply stop, and it's not self-harm in the usual sense; it's a condition with its own treatment, and shame is usually the heaviest part.
what_it_can_feel_like: I'd come out of a film and realize my lap was covered in hair. I hadn't noticed a single pull.
No swimming, no wind, no one touching my head. I built my whole life around hiding it.
The TLC group was the first time I'd met anyone else who did it. I cried the whole call.
common_signs: Repeatedly pulling out hair, leading to visible hair loss
Repeated attempts to stop or cut down
Pulling that happens automatically, or in a focused way to relieve an urge
Hiding hair loss with styles, makeup, hats, or avoiding activities
Distress, shame, or trouble at work, school, or socially

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's just a nervous habit. Snap out of it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Trichotillomania involves brain pathways for habit and reward. Willpower alone rarely works; a specific behavioural therapy does.
Most people with trich aren't trying to hurt themselves. Pulling often soothes, relieves tension, or happens without awareness.
Around 1 to 2 in 100 people have it. Almost all of them think they're the only one.

how_common.plain: About 1 to 2 in every 100 people have trichotillomania at some point. It usually starts around puberty and is diagnosed more often in women, though in childhood it affects boys and girls equally.
how_common.figure: Estimated 1%–2% 12-month prevalence (DSM-5-TR text); a 2020 US survey found about 1.7% of adults
how_common.note: Grant et al. 2020 figure seen in query only; needs a primary citation.

what_helps.plain_summary: The best-supported treatment is habit reversal training, usually within a broader behavioural therapy for BFRBs: becoming aware of the pulling, using a competing action when the urge comes, and changing the situations that trigger it. Approaches that add acceptance and emotion skills help too. Medication has limited evidence; a doctor may consider options and monitors them. Peer support is unusually powerful for this condition because the shame is so heavy.
evidence_based_options: Habit reversal training and comprehensive behavioural therapy for BFRBs
Acceptance-based and DBT-informed additions for urges and emotions
Treatment of co-occurring anxiety or depression
Medication in some cases, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, with limited evidence
self_help_that_supports_care: Tracking when, where, and how pulling happens
Fiddle toys, gloves, or bandages at high-risk times, without shame
Changing the setting: lighting, mirrors, screens, positions
Joining a BFRB support group, online or in person

when_to_reach_out: If pulling is causing hair loss you have to hide, or you've tried to stop and can't, a therapist trained in BFRBs can help. Dermatologists and GPs can also check for any skin or scalp issues and point you to support.
is_not: Twirling or occasionally pulling hair without hair loss isn't the disorder. Hair loss from alopecia or medical causes needs a different assessment, though the two can co-exist.
hope_note: Trichotillomania is treatable, and the moment people find others who pull, the shame starts to lift.
in_young_people: In very young children, hair pulling often fades on its own. From around puberty it tends to persist and needs treatment. Teens may avoid swimming, PE, and sleepovers; telling the school discreetly helps.
